title: Seven days
hookLine: mourners stay home seven days; visitors bring food and sit with them
last: FILLING THE GRAVE IS THE KINDNESS OF TRUTH.

cards: What do you say to someone whose mother was buried this morning? The book of Job has a strange answer. Job has lost his children, his wealth, his health.
Three friends travel to him. When they see him, they weep and tear their clothes.
Then, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, they sit with him on the ground "seven days and seven nights", and nobody says a word, because they can see how great his grief is.
Some readers say it's the best thing those friends do in the whole book.

teach.b: Shiva means seven. You first met Job's silent friends back in year three; today, the week itself. First, the seven days.

When Joseph buries his father Jacob, Genesis says "he made a mourning for his father seven days." Jewish mourning keeps that week. After the funeral the closest family stay home and sit low, on low chairs or cushions.
In some homes mirrors are covered. Work stops, and the world comes to them. Second, the silence.
The Talmud learns from Job's friends that comforters don't speak first.

teach.h: WAIT FOR THE MOURNER TO SPEAK.
teach.b: You come in, sit, and wait for the mourner to open. If they want to talk about the person who died, you listen. If they want silence, you give it.
You don't have to find the right sentence; the tradition takes that job away from you. Third, the food.
The mourners don't cook the first meal after the burial; neighbors and friends bring it.
All week people keep arriving with soup and bread and trays nobody asked for, and in some homes a group gathers each day so the mourners can say Kaddish without leaving the house.
Leaving, visitors say a traditional line asking that God comfort the mourners among all who mourn for Zion and Jerusalem.
Fourth, the week just past: the holy society, the washing and the shroud, plain wood, the tear, God full of mercy, the shovel, and now seven days of company.
Step by step, the dead are honored, and then the living are not left alone.

how: After a Jewish funeral, the closest mourners stay home for shiva, sitting low; friends and neighbors bring meals, visit, and often gather so the mourners can say Kaddish at home, and visitors traditionally wait for the mourner to speak first.

games.q: you walk into a shiva house. the mourner sits on a low chair and says nothing. what does tradition say you do first?
o: sit down, and wait for the mourner to speak.
start telling a story about the person who died.
games.why: you sit and wait. the tradition, learning from Job's friends, lets the mourner open the conversation, or keep the silence.

practice: Picture someone who is grieving, now or not long ago, and yourself sitting near them, low, saying nothing: no advice, no sentence about better places or reasons, only your company.

Let the quiet be the gift, and if you pray, hold them in your prayer. And if the grief is your own and it feels like too much, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Shiva. Seven: the week the mourners stay home, and the world brings food and sits with them. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: seven, the week of mourning at home.

carryVoice: Your line: sit with them. Your company says what no sentence can. See you tomorrow.
